job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Erik Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my parents in Ridgemont. My father runs a small building firm, and my uncle Chidi manages a bank branch downtown, so money talk is the family sport. I'm up at seven, put on a shirt and tie even at home, and spend the morning on applications for bank trainee schemes. I finished a finance degree at Ridgemont University last summer, with a pass and no internship. In the afternoon I help my father with his quotes and invoices, and on Sundays we're all at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's fine, a useful bit of automation and no more. A good worker will always be needed, and the old rules about reliability and honest work still hold. I wouldn't change my plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm a bit restless. Several months without an offer is not what I pictured. My uncle says banks recruit through their own schemes, and the next intake is in spring. I'm trusting that, but waiting isn't easy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply to the spring bank schemes, and in the meantime do a few things properly. I'd study for a basic banking certificate on weekday evenings. I'd keep handling my father's invoices, which is real bookkeeping. And I'd keep attending my uncle's branch events, to be known.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, I'd say. I'm grateful for my family, and I don't take it for granted. I'm not scared, just impatient to start my own working life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your uncle manages a bank branch. Has he helped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's helped by telling me honestly how it works. He can't recommend me directly, because it's against the bank's rules, and I respect that. But he told me which certificates matter and who to speak to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a good first year look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be doing a real job in a real team by October, learning from someone who knows more than me. I'd be paying my parents a bit for the room. That would feel like starting.

think: I'm a bit **restless**, since several months without an offer isn't what I pictured.

do: Apply to the **spring bank schemes** and study for a basic banking certificate in the evenings.

Attend my uncle's branch **events** to be known.
feel: **Steady** and grateful for family, but impatient to start my own working life.

Worry is the wait, not AI.

steps.text: Apply to the spring bank trainee schemes

Handle my father's invoices and quotes properly

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should be sensible. Technology has always changed work, and the answer is training and hard work, not complaints. Banks should keep taking trainees, because that's how they get good managers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm a bit worried. My uncle says the branch already handles fewer cash transactions and fewer loan checks by hand. Trainee posts are being reviewed. That's exactly where I'm trying to enter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try a couple of AI tools at my father's firm, for quotes and cost checks, so I can say I've used them in real work. I'd also apply to smaller finance firms, credit unions and insurers, not only banks. I'd carry on with the certificate, and keep up the church community, which is a network too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a practical way. It's like seeing the weather turn. I don't panic, I check the roof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bank jobs would shrink first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cash handling, basic loan checks, standard reports, call-centre type questions. The people who stay are those who manage relationships, like my uncle, who knows every business owner in town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you rather wait for proof or move now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Move, carefully. I'm not someone who jumps first, but I've seen that waiting for proof can mean waiting too long. If I can try something small in a safe setting, like my father's quotes, I'll do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're not ready and we should be honest about that. Families, churches and employers will carry a lot of the weight, so they should be involved early. And governments shouldn't just hand out money, they should help people work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm afraid. Banking is thinking work, so it goes first. My degree is the thing my parents were proud of, and now it might be worth little. Meanwhile my father's building work lasts longer, until the robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a job at my father's firm, doing the office side and learning the site side. I'd ask to be trained as a site supervisor. I'd save as much as I can, and cut spending on anything extra. And I'd keep applying to finance firms, in case some roles remain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and a bit ashamed, which is silly. I'd pray, and talk to my pastor. I'd feel the weight of being the first in the family to go to university and then, maybe, not use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your uncle that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, Uncle, tell me honestly what you see. He'd say the branch will shrink, that he's not sure he's safe himself. That would hit me hard, because I thought he was the solid one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is different if the robots arrive in 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Building work lasts about three more years than office work. That's why I'd start on site now. It's not a plan forever, but it buys time to see what else emerges.

say: We're not ready, and **families, churches and employers** will carry much of the weight.
Governments should help people work, not only hand out money.
think: I'm afraid, because banking is thinking work and goes first, and my **degree** may be worth little.
My father's building work lasts longer.

fieldNote: He uses the **three-year robot gap** directly to pick hands-on work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough if people act sensibly. Families should talk about it, employers should train, and the state should help apprenticeships. I'd mention it at church and to my father's workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be uneasy but not scared. If I get a job in the next year, I'd have time to move into advising small businesses. My father's customers need someone who can read a budget. That's work with trust in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the first finance or trainee job offered, learn the tools there, and keep helping my father. I'd save about a third of my pay. I'd study for a recognised qualification, and in year three I'd decide whether to stay in finance or move toward project management in construction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, like having a deadline on the calendar. It's good to know when, even if you don't like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years. Is that enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My uncle, my father, and the pastor. Each tells me something different. My uncle says about banks, my father says about work, the pastor says about people. I need all three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you ask for advice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me one decision point in year three. That's about right. Two would be a scramble, and ten might make me too relaxed.

say: Five years is enough if people act sensibly: **employers train** and the state backs apprenticeships.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is a good warning, and we should use it to build skills and good habits. Young people should learn both a trade and a profession. I'd say that to anyone who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm calm about it. By 2036 I'd be 33, with a career, probably a family, and a house. Ten years lets me build proper foundations. The change would be big, but I'd be older and sturdier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get a bank or finance job, qualify, and work my way up slowly. I'd save toward a house, and invest a little each month. I'd keep helping my father's firm, and learn how AI tools work in both banking and building.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's a distant date, and my life will have plenty to do before then. I'd keep it in view, the way you keep an eye on the weather.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years. What's the main thing it changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd do the same. Study, work, save, pray. It's the steady way. But I'd be more careful not to rely on one employer, because they can change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you do anything differently now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My answer is the same as for the long scenarios. Don't rush, don't ignore it. Build a base that holds in more than one weather.

think: I'm **calm**: by 2036 I'd be 33 with a career, probably a family and a house.

S4.quote: Build a base that holds in more than one weather.
fieldNote: His calm rests on **routine and family**, not on trusting the technology.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. It arrives before families, churches and employers can prepare, and my degree is the thing my parents were proudest of. What would help is real apprenticeship places, banks that keep taking trainees, and honest advice from people like my uncle.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm grateful for my family, and I know many graduates don't have that. I'd hope any plan helps those who can't lean on a father's firm or an uncle's advice.

headlineQuote: I'm grateful for my family, and I know many graduates don't have that.
portrait: Erik is a **23-year-old** finance graduate in Ridgemont, son of a builder and nephew of a bank manager.
He is **traditional**: faith, family, hard work and apprenticeships guide him, and he prefers training to handouts.
He is a **steady** adapter who tries AI tools in small safe settings, such as his father's quotes.
The 2028 world makes him **anxious**, and he uses the three-year robot gap to move to site work.
With more time he builds decision points, qualifications and savings.
biggestWorry: His biggest worry is **AGI by 2028**, which arrives before families, churches and employers can prepare.
whatWouldHelp: Real **apprenticeship places**, banks that keep taking trainees, and honest advice from people who know the field.
